paper_title: PreSTO: Predictive Subtree Prefetching for Fast LLM Power Sampling

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Power sampling improves large language model (LLM) reasoning at test time by sampling from a sharpened version of the base model's distribution. Its sampler, PowerMH, is slow because its Metropolis--Hastings (MH) updates are sequential: each accept/reject decision sets the state from which the next proposal is generated. Prior work reduces this cost by changing the sampler or the model (e.g., sequential Monte Carlo, approximate lookahead, distillation). We propose Predictive SubTree Prefetching (PreSTO), which accelerates PowerMH by prefetching future proposals and provably leaves its MH transition kernel unchanged. PreSTO views future MH outcomes as a tree of accept/reject decisions: in each model call, it generates the proposals of a \textit{prefetched subtree} of this tree in one batch, then follows the realized path with the original MH acceptance rule. We also observe that MH reaches only a sparse, nearly unary part of each prefetched subtree, we further design a \textit{predictive traversal rule} that chooses the subtree to maximize the predicted number of completed transitions. Across seven datasets and five base LLMs, PreSTO achieves median speedups of $1.71\times$, $1.91\times$, and $2.33\times$ on PowerMH and its follow-ups EntropyCut and MultiTryMH, respectively; on the first two, it makes a median of $3.9\times$ fewer model calls, each only $2.1\times$ longer. On LCB V6 with Qwen3.5-9B, the predictive traversal rule is a further $1.25\times$--$1.37\times$ faster than the default breadth-first traversal.

Introduction Large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on reasoning tasks such as competition mathematics, code generation, and graduate-level science questions (Hendrycks et al., 2021b; Li et al., 2022; Rein et al., 2024). These capabilities are commonly improved by reinforcement learning (RL) post-training with task-specific rewards (Guo et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025). Recent work suggests that RL posttraining largely sharpens the base models distribution (Chen et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2026), and that sampling directly from sharpened distribution, known as power sampling, can perform comparably to RL post-training without additional training (Karan and Du, 2026). Figure 1 Across 105 samplerLLMdataset settings, PreSTO (ours) speeds up PowerMH, EntropyCut, and MultiTryMH by median of 1.71, 1.91, and 2.33, respectively. Each point is one setting, and faster settings lie toward the upper right. Corresponding Author: njiang@utep.edu 2 However, PowerMH, the MetropolisHastings (MH) sampler for power sampling, is expensive (Ji et al., 2026): on MATH500, it generates up to 8.8 as many tokens as standard sampling (Karan and Du, 2026), and on LCB V6 with Qwen3.5-9B, it takes 6.518.4 as long per prompt as singlesample low-temperature sampling (Case Study 8, Appendix E.8). Follow-up work improves it in four directions: (1) Alternative samplers replace serial MH with sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) or replica exchange (Azizi et al., 2026; He et al., 2026). (2) Efficient approximations of the power target reduce inference cost (Ji et al., 2026; Nguyen et al., 2026). (3) Proposal refinements choose cut indices by token-level entropy to improve mixing (Guo et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026). (4) Objective or training changes target the answer marginal (Arzhantsev et al., 2026) or fine-tune the model on power-sampled responses (Tomihari and Sato, 2026). The main bottleneck of PowerMH is the sequential dependence between MH transitions: in standard implementation, each proposal must be accepted or rejected before the next is generated from the resulting state. We draw on prefetching in classical MCMC (Angelino et al., 2014; Brockwell, 2006): future MH transitions form tree of accept/reject outcomes, and each sequential run traces one root-to-leaf path. If the proposals on this path are available in advance, several transitions complete without another model call. We present Predictive SubTree Prefetching (PreSTO), framework for accelerating MH-based sharpened sampling by completing several MH transitions per model call. In each round, PreSTO builds prefetched subtree, generates its feasible proposals in one batched model call, and follows the realized path with the original MH acceptance rule. We prove that PreSTO-PowerMH leaves the MH transition kernel of PowerMH unchanged (Proposition 1). We further observe that, under the power-sharpened target, MH reaches only sparse, nearly unary part of each prefetched subtree (Figure 4 and Appendix E.4), so breadth-first traversal spends much of the budget on nodes that MH rarely visits. Motivated by this, we propose improved predictive traversal rule that allocates the prefetch budget to maximize the expected number of MH transitions completed per call. PreSTO trades fewer serial calls for costlier batched call; with prefix-cache reuse across requests, total latency falls whenever the saved calls outweigh the extra cost per batch. In experiments, we apply PreSTO to PowerMH, EntropyCut, and MultiTryMH on seven datasets and five base LLMs. PreSTO is never slower than its baseline in all 105 settings, with median speedups of 1.71 over PowerMH, 1.91 over EntropyCut, and 2.33 over MultiTryMH, and maximum speedups of 2.29 and 2.85 over the first two (Figure 1). Our case studies show that (1) the speedup comes from fewer model calls rather than cheaper ones: over PowerMH, PreSTO-PowerMH makes 1.944.92 fewer calls, each taking 1.903.42 as long (Figure 1); (2) the log-likelihood and confidence of PreSTO outputs pass paired equivalence tests against the baselines in 29 of 38 comparisons, which supports that PreSTO leaves the MH transition kernel unchanged (Figure 6); and (3) the predictive traversal rule is 1.251.37 faster than the default breadth-first search (BFS) traversal at all five prefetch budgets tested on LCB V6 with Qwen3.5-9B (Figure 7). 2. Related Work We review related work most relevant to PreSTO here; see Appendix for an extended discussion. MCMC prefetching. Like prior MCMC-prefetching methods (Angelino et al., 2014; Brockwell, 2006; Ye and Lu, 2024), PreSTO precomputes candidates for future accept/reject outcomes before the realized path is known. The methods differ in how they allocate this speculative work. Brockwell (2006) and Angelino et al. (2014) treat proposal generation as cheap and therefore prefetch many more candidates than the chain eventually uses. LLM proposals are expensive, so PreSTO confines prefetching to budgeted subtree. Ye and Lu (2024) expand regular multiproposal tree with fixed number of proposals and fixed prefetch depth, whereas PreSTO expands an irregular subtree: it uses Condition 1 to identify feasible suffix requests and prioritizes them by predicted reach probability. Tree-based speculative decoding (TreeSD) (Cai et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024a,b; Miao et al., 2024) also batches evaluations over tree to reduce serial model calls, but its tree encodes different objects. In TreeSD, branches are alternative draft-token continuations, and target-model verification commits an accepted token prefix, as in single-chain speculative decoding (Chen et al., 2023; Leviathan et al., 2023; Stern et al., 2018). In PreSTO, branches are the accept/reject outcomes of complete-sequence MH proposals, and following the realized MH decisions reproduces the sequential PowerMH trajectory. The shared tree structure admits similar budget-allocation arguments, but the unit of progress differs: each visited expanded node in PreSTO advances the chain by one MH transition, whether the proposal is accepted or rejected. Power-sharpening methods. Other work targets the power distribution through SMC-based samplers (Azizi et al., 2026; He et al., 2026), efficient approximations (Ji et al., 2026; Nguyen et al., 2026), refined proposals (Guo et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026), or modified objectives and training procedures (Arzhantsev et al., 2026; Tomihari and Sato, 2026). Conclusion We study how to accelerate MH-based power sampling, whose sequential accept/reject decisions force one model call per MH transition. We propose PreSTO, which prefetches proposals for subtree of future MH states in one batched call and follows the realized path with the original acceptance rule; for PowerMH, this leaves the MH transition kernel unchanged (Proposition 1). Because the part of prefetched subtree reached by MH is sparse and nearly unary, our predictive traversal rule allocates the prefetch budget by dynamic programming. In experiments, across five base LLMs and seven datasets, PreSTO is never slower than its baseline and achieves median speedups of 1.71 over PowerMH, 1.91 over EntropyCut, and 2.33 over MultiTryMH. The speedup comes from fewer model calls, at cost of at most 3.1% of the preallocated KV-cache pool, and the log-likelihood and confidence of the outputs pass paired equivalence tests against the baselines in 29 of 38 comparisons. The predictive traversal rule adds further 1.251.37 speedup over the default BFS traversal on LCB V6 with Qwen3.5-9B.

Extended Related Work PreSTO draws on three lines of work. Power-sampling methods define the target and the samplers that PreSTO accelerates. Speculative decoding and MCMC prefetching are two established ways to break serial dependence during sampling. For each line, we summarize the problem it addresses, the mechanism its methods share, and the trade-offs among them. A.1. Sampling from the Power Distribution Power sampling draws complete responses from 𝜋𝛼 𝑝𝛼 with 𝛼 > 1 (Karan and Du, 2026). Raising 0 the sequence likelihood to power concentrates probability on responses that the base model finds likely as whole, the same construction that annealing and parallel tempering use to control how concentrated target is (Neal, 2001; Sambridge, 2014). Why token-level sharpening is not enough. Token-level temperature scaling and filtering (Du et al., 2025; Troshin et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2024) sharpen each next-token distribution and renormalize at every prefix. The exact next-token conditional of the power target is instead 𝜋𝛼(𝑥𝑡 x0:𝑡1) 𝑝0(𝑥𝑡 x0:𝑡1)𝛼 𝑍𝛼(x0:𝑡), where 𝑍𝛼(x0:𝑡) = 𝑝0(x𝑡+1:𝑛 x0:𝑡)𝛼. x𝑡+1:𝑛 Token-level temperature 𝜏 = 1/𝛼 keeps the first factor and drops 𝑍𝛼. For 𝛼 > 1, 𝑍𝛼 is large when the continuations of prefix concentrate on few high-likelihood completions, so the power target prefers such prefixes, whereas low-temperature decoding cannot distinguish them. Because 𝑍𝛼 sums over exponentially many continuations, every power-sampling method must avoid it, approximate it, or change the target. Existing methods follow three routes. MCMC over complete sequences. MH needs the target only up to constant, so it avoids 𝑍𝛼 entirely: it compares complete sequences through the ratio 𝜋𝛼(y)/𝜋𝛼(x) = (cid:0) 𝑝0(y)/𝑝0(x)(cid:1) 𝛼. The main design choice is the proposal. Earlier MCMC samplers for controlled generation with energybased targets edit one position at time and need many steps to make coordinated changes across sequence (Mireshghallah et al., 2022). Regenerating complete sequence or suffix with an LLM instead makes large, coherent edits whose proposal probabilities come from the same forward pass (Faria et al., 2024; Forristal et al., 2023). PowerMH applies suffix regeneration to 𝜋𝛼 with blockwise schedule (Karan and Du, 2026), and later variants keep this structure while changing where cuts are placed or how many candidates each step considers. EntropyCut (Zhou et al., 2026) places cuts using token entropy, and MultiTryMH, variant of the entropy-guided sampler of Guo et al. (2026), draws several candidate suffixes per step and moves with multiple-try Metropolis update (Liu et al., 2000). Other variants add terms to the target (Meng et al., 2026). These samplers share three costs: each transition regenerates on average about half of the response when the cut is uniform, each stage needs many transitions, and transitions are serial because every proposal is conditioned on the current state. Forward approximations. Forward methods generate left to right and estimate 𝑍𝛼 rather than drop it. Particle methods propagate population of partial sequences from tractable proposal, such as low-temperature decoding, reweight them at every step by the ratio of target to proposal, and resample to discard low-weight prefixes. Without twisting, these intermediate weights ignore the future term 𝑍𝛼; twisted variants learn approximations of 𝑍𝛼 so that the intermediate weights account for it (Zhao et al., 2024). For power targets, these samplers are consistent as the number of particles grows (Azizi et al., 2026; He et al., 2026), and in practice their quality depends on resampling rules that prevent weight degeneracy and particle collapse (Ahmadi et al., 2026). Lookahead methods instead estimate 𝑍𝛼(x0:𝑡) directly by sampling few continuations for each candidate token, and use 20 the estimate to correct the next-token distribution (Ji et al., 2026; Nguyen et al., 2026). Both families parallelize naturally across particles or rollouts. Their bias and variance, however, depend on the number of particles or rollouts, and they never revise token; resampling only drops or duplicates whole prefixes. Changing or amortizing the target. third route changes what is sampled or moves the cost into training. Sharpening the sequence likelihood can favor single high-likelihood reasoning trace over an answer supported by many distinct traces, so marginal sharpening sharpens the distribution over final answers instead (Arzhantsev et al., 2026). Distillation-style methods fine-tune the model so that ordinary sampling approximates powered or low-temperature sequence distribution, which removes the inference-time overhead at the price of training (Scheufele et al., 2026; Tomihari and Sato, 2026). Evidence on when sharpening helps is mixed: raising sequence likelihood through decoding need not improve correctness (Zenn and Geiping, 2026), and reward-trained models can gain in ways that sharpening does not recover (Mittal et al., 2026). A.2. Tree-based Speculative Decoding Tree-based speculative decoding (TreeSD) is the closest counterpart to PreSTO in the speculativedecoding literature, because it also spends extra parallel computation on work that may be discarded in order to reduce the number of serial model calls. We first describe the draft-then-verify scheme that TreeSD builds on, then how trees extend it, and finally how PreSTO differs. Draft-then-verify decoding. Autoregressive decoding calls the target model once per token, and these calls cannot be batched because each token depends on the previous one. Speculative decoding breaks this dependence with cheap drafter that proposes several future tokens (Stern et al., 2018; Xia et al., 2024). The target model then scores all of them in single forward pass, and verification rule commits the longest accepted prefix together with one token drawn from corrected distribution (Chen et al., 2023; Leviathan et al., 2023). With the rejection-based rule, the committed tokens follow the target models distribution exactly, so drafter quality affects only speed. Every pass commits at least one token, and the expected number of tokens committed per pass grows with the drafters acceptance rate. Drafting tree of continuations. chain of draft tokens is truncated at its first rejected token, so one early rejection wastes all later draft work. Tree-based methods instead draft several alternative continuations at each position, and verify all branches in one pass with tree-structured attention mask, so that each branch attends only to its own ancestors (Miao et al., 2024). The target model can then commit whichever branch is accepted furthest, which raises the expected number of tokens committed per pass at the cost of scoring more candidate tokens. In all of these methods, the nodes of the tree are draft tokens, the branching reflects uncertainty about what the target model will say next, and verification pass ends with single committed prefix. Better drafters. second line of work raises the acceptance rate of the drafter itself. Extra decoding heads attached to the target model draft several positions at once without separate drafter model (Cai et al., 2024), and autoregression at the level of the target models features gives drafter that tracks the target more closely (Li et al., 2024b). Better drafters shift the balance between how many tokens are drafted and how many are accepted, and so change which tree shapes are worth verifying. Tree construction as budget allocation. For fixed verification budget, i.e., fixed number of nodes per pass, tree can take many shapes, so tree construction is budget-allocation problem. Early methods use static shape (Cai et al., 2024; Miao et al., 2024). Later methods add branches where the drafter is confident, since those nodes are more likely to be accepted (Li et al., 2024a), or choose the tree shape by dynamic programming over estimated acceptance rates (Chen et al., 2024). These 21 approaches share one principle: under node budget, expand the nodes whose expected contribution to the committed prefix is largest. Relaxing exact verification. Exact rejection is not the only option. SMC-based variants weight and resample draft blocks instead of truncating at the first rejected token. They accept finite-particle approximation in exchange for using more of the drafted work, and have been applied to power targets (Emara et al., 2026). This differs from PreSTO in that the output is no longer exact for the target, whereas PreSTO preserves the PowerMH trajectory. Relation to PreSTO. PreSTO and TreeSD both use tree to batch evaluations that would otherwise be serial, both leave the law of the underlying sampler unchanged (for PreSTO-PowerMH, the law of the PowerMH chain, not 𝜋𝛼 itself), and both face the same question of where to spend limited speculative budget, so TreeSDs budget-allocation arguments carry over to our setting. The two trees encode different objects, however. In TreeSD, branch is an alternative draft-token continuation, and verification commits an accepted token prefix. In PreSTO, branch is an accept/reject outcome of complete-sequence MH proposal, and following the realized MH decisions reproduces the sequential PowerMH trajectory. The unit of progress also differs: every visited expanded node in PreSTO advances the chain by one MH transition, whether the proposal is accepted or rejected, while TreeSD node contributes only if it lies on the accepted prefix. Finally, the cost structure differs. In TreeSD, cheap drafter proposes the nodes, and only the target models verification pass is expensive. PreSTO has no cheap drafter: every node is full suffix that the proposal LLM must generate, the same work as one sequential PowerMH proposal. Expanding the full tree would spend most of this work on nodes off the realized path, so PreSTO confines speculation to budgeted subtree. A.3. MCMC Prefetching Parallel MCMC methods typically run many independent chains, parallelize the evaluation of the target density, or speculate on the future of single chain. Prefetching is the third approach (Brockwell, 2006; Strid, 2010). It rests on one observation: from any state, the next 𝑑 accept/reject outcomes form binary tree of depth 𝑑, and the chain follows exactly one root-to-leaf path. Proposals for every node can be drawn in advance, so the expensive target evaluations at all nodes can run in parallel. The realized path is then read off with the usual acceptance uniforms, so the chain has exactly the law of sequential MH. Evaluating the whole tree is wasteful. It has 2𝑑 1 decision nodes, of which only 𝑑 lie on the realized path, so the speedup obtained from 𝑝 parallel workers grows only logarithmically in 𝑝 (Brockwell, 2006). Later methods therefore evaluate only the nodes most likely to lie on the realized path. Static prefetching uses the acceptance rate: when acceptance is low, rejection branches dominate, and the tree can be restricted to long rejection chains (Strid, 2010). Predictive prefetching uses cheap approximation of the target to estimate each branch probability, and still decides every realized transition with the exact target (Angelino et al., 2014). different approach parallelizes within one transition by drawing several candidates from the current state, whose target evaluations can run in parallel. Multiple-try Metropolis selects one candidate with probability proportional to its weight and accepts or rejects it with corrected acceptance probability (Liu et al., 2000). Multiproposal MH instead moves according to Markov chain over the candidate set (Calderhead, 2014). Both preserve the stationary distribution but change the transition kernel. Multiproposal steps can be combined with prefetching by expanding tree of multiproposal steps (Ye and Lu, 2024). MultiTryMH (Guo et al., 2026) applies multiple-try Metropolis to 𝜋𝛼, drawing its candidate suffixes in parallel; PreSTO is complementary to this within-transition parallelism, and PreSTO-MultiTryMH prefetches across MultiTryMH transitions. We apply PreSTO to three MH-based samplers that target the same power distribution, and compare each sampler with its PreSTO variant: PowerMH (Karan and Du, 2026) builds continuation block by block. At each block, it extends the current prefix with the proposal LLM and then runs several MH updates that target the powersharpened distribution over the extended prefix. Each update draws cut position uniformly at random, keeps the tokens before it, resamples the suffix from the proposal LLM, and accepts or rejects the candidate with the MH correction. It regenerates the suffix from the chosen position and applies the MH correction, so the power target is preserved. MultiTryMH replaces each single-proposal PowerMH update with Multiple-Try Metropolis update (Liu et al., 2000). Case Study 7: Predicting 𝜖-certainty before generation The predictive traversal rule (Appendix C.3) needs the class probabilities (cid:98)𝑃(𝑣 is 𝜖-certain reject) and (cid:98)𝑃(𝑣 is 𝜖-certain accept) of every candidate node 𝑣 before the proposal at 𝑣+ is generated. We therefore predict, from information available before generation, which of the three classes of Section 3.3 each candidate node falls into: certain reject (𝐴 𝜖), certain accept (𝐴 1 𝜖), or uncertain (𝜖 < 𝐴 < 1 𝜖). We use the results to choose the input features and the model of the rule. Setting. Each run records the acceptance probability 𝐴 = 𝐴(𝑣+, 𝑣) of every prefetched node, and these nodes are the examples. We use one run per sampler, on the first 20 prompts of LCB V6 with Qwen3.5-9B. The PreSTO-PowerMH dataset has 4,621 nodes from 579 model calls: 2,814 𝜖-certain rejects, 945 𝜖-certain accepts, and 862 𝜖-uncertain. The PreSTO-EntropyCut dataset has 4,533 nodes from 568 model calls: 2,701, 880, and 952, respectively. These are about 8 nodes per call, fewer than 𝑁pf = 10, for two reasons. First, the calls issue 5,690 and 5,546 requests; we drop the 1,069 and 1,013 requests that BFS places below the rejection child of node whose acceptance-child request it deferred under Condition 1, because the MH walk of that call stops at that node and does not reach them. Second, 21 and 22 calls near the end of prompt, when at most 6 of the 𝐾 transitions remain, issue fewer than 10 requests. Because the examples are the nodes that BFS actually prefetched, they follow the distribution of the prefetched subtree, not that of all candidate nodes. We group the features, all available when the batch is assembled, into four sets: Feature 1 (cut fraction): the cut fraction 𝑐 𝑗/𝑇 of the request, where 𝑣𝑗 is the acceptance child of the node 𝑣𝑖 (that is, 𝑣𝑖 = 𝑣 and 𝑣 𝑗 = 𝑣+). Feature 2 (tree position): the cut index 𝑐𝑖 of 𝑣𝑖, the gap 𝑐𝑖 𝑐 𝑗, the depth of 𝑣𝑖, and the number of acceptances on the path from the root to 𝑣𝑖. Feature 3 (likelihood): four statistics of the token-wise log-likelihood of the root state under the proposal LLM: its value at the first resampled token, its changes into and out of that token, and its mean over the suffix after the cut. 49 Feature 4 (entropy, PreSTO-EntropyCut only): the same four statistics of the token-wise entropy of the root state; the uniform-cut run did not log token entropies. Case Study 8: Comparison with test-time baselines PreSTO-PowerMH speeds up PowerMH without changing its transition kernel, but PowerMH is only one way to spend test-time compute. This case study places both among three baselines that also sharpen the base distribution or select among samples: low-temperature sampling, best-of-𝑁 (Stiennon et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2024), and PowerSMC (Azizi et al., 2026). Low-temperature sampling and best-of-𝑁 do not target 𝑝𝛼 : scaling each tokens logits by 𝛼 renormalizes every conditional separately, 0 which differs from the sequence-level power distribution (Karan and Du, 2026). We compare their generation time, peak KV-pool use, and accuracy on the same prompts. Setting. All runs use the first 20 prompts of LCB V6 with Qwen3.5-9B, process one prompt at time on vLLM, and target 𝛼 = 4. PowerMH and PreSTO-PowerMH ignore the end-of-sequence token and always generate all 1,024 new tokens, whereas low-temperature sampling, best-of-𝑁, and PowerSMC stop sample at the end-of-sequence token, so they generate up to 1,024 new tokens. PowerMH and PreSTO-PowerMH run single block of 𝐾 {10, 20, 30} MH transitions, fewer than the 𝐾 = 100 of the main runs, and PreSTO-PowerMH uses the default BFS traversal at 𝑁pf = 10. Low-temperature sampling draws one sample at temperature 1/𝛼 = 0.25; best-of-𝑁 draws 𝑁 {4, 8, 16, 32} samples at the same temperature and keeps the one with the highest unnormalized sequence log-probability, the sum of its token log-probabilities under this temperature-0.25 sampling distribution rather than under 𝑝0. PowerSMC grows 𝑃 {2, 4, 8, 16, 32} particles in blocks of 128 tokens, resamples when the effective sample size falls below half, and ramps the exponent to 𝛼 over the first 400 tokens. Time is the generation time per prompt, excluding model loading and grading, and peak KV-pool use is the largest fraction of the preallocated KV pool in use. Figure 20 plots peak KV-pool use against time. Figure 20 Speed and memory against test-time baselines. Peak KV-pool use against time per prompt on the first 20 prompts of LCB V6 with Qwen3.5-9B; lower left is better. Results. Figure 20 shows that prefetching raises peak KV-pool use, but by less than the parallel baselines at their larger settings. Best-of-𝑁 and PowerSMC decode all samples or particles at once, so their peak KV-pool use grows with 𝑁 or 𝑃, reaching 12.7% of the pool at 𝑁 = 32 and 8.5% at 𝑃 = 32. PreSTO-PowerMH batches 10 proposals and peaks at 2.9%3.1% at every 𝐾, close to best-of-8 (3.3%), compared with 0.6% for PowerMH. PreSTO-PowerMH therefore narrows, but does not close, the cost gap between PowerMH and these baselines. 52 E.9. Example prefetched-subtree trajectory We print the raw log of one prefetched subtree. Each line of the log is node 𝑣𝑖, printed as Node(id=𝑖, cut_idx=𝑐𝑖). Node 𝑣𝑖 has acceptance child 𝑣2𝑖+1 and rejection child 𝑣2𝑖+2; the rejection child keeps its parents state and cut index. Each acceptance edge carries log_mh_ratio, the unclamped log MH ratio of the proposal at 𝑣2𝑖+1, so the edge is taken with probability min{1, exp(log_mh_ratio)}; rejection edges carry no value. The tree holds 16 of the 20 requests in the batch.
